final.title: Escalation paths get clearer when you name one rule
final.body:
If you want to rethink escalation paths, start with one recurring workflow, not the whole business. Pick the place where decisions keep getting passed around by email, chat, or memory: customer questions, invoice review, lead triage, or something similar. Then write the current rule in plain English: who decides, what the trigger is, and what happens next when the first person cannot decide. That is often the real problem. The hidden rule is usually there; it is just living in people’s heads.

The next step is a simple yes-or-no filter. Ask whether the escalation rule is explicit, whether the inputs are digital and structured enough to handle reliably, and whether the cost of a wrong decision is low enough to keep moving. If the answer is no, do not force automation. Use a checklist, routing template, or delegation rule instead, and keep human approval in place for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

If the answer is yes, you have a candidate for a narrow pilot later. If not, you still get something useful: a clearer handoff and fewer decisions lost in email archaeology.
